summary: How motor commands leave the brain for skeletal muscle and viscera, and how sensory signals from the body wall and organs get back in. Exam questions ask you to place a lesion by sorting upper from lower motor neuron signs and by matching a pattern of lost tracts to a named spinal cord syndrome.

points: Starts in the precentral gyrus (primary motor cortex), with help from premotor cortex; Betz cells sit in layer V.
Path: corona radiata, posterior limb of the internal capsule, middle part of the cerebral peduncle, basilar pons, medullary pyramid.
About 85 to 90 percent of fibers cross at the pyramidal decussation in the caudal medulla and run in the lateral funiculus as the lateral corticospinal tract.
Fibers end on anterior horn alpha motor neurons (directly or through interneurons), whose axons leave in the ventral root to skeletal muscle.
The uncrossed remainder forms the anterior corticospinal tract for axial muscles.
Lesion above the decussation gives contralateral weakness; lesion in the cord gives ipsilateral weakness below the level.
notes.why: The corticospinal axons funnel tightly through the posterior limb of the internal capsule, so a small lacune there can cause dense hemiparesis. Because most fibers cross in the caudal medulla, the decussation is the reference point for laterality: above it the weakness is contralateral, and in the cord it is ipsilateral to the lesion. The tract ends on the anterior horn alpha motor neuron, the final common pathway, so every lesion above that synapse is upper motor neuron and every lesion from the anterior horn cell outward is lower motor neuron.

points: UMN lesion (cortex, capsule, brainstem, cord tract): spastic tone, brisk reflexes, Babinski sign, little atrophy.
LMN lesion (anterior horn, root, nerve): flaccid weakness, reduced reflexes, fasciculations, marked atrophy.
ALS: loss of both UMNs and anterior horn cells, so both sets of signs appear together; sensation, eye movements, and sphincters are usually spared.
Poliomyelitis: poliovirus destroys anterior horn cells, giving asymmetric flaccid paralysis with pure LMN signs.
Spinal muscular atrophy: autosomal recessive SMN1 loss causes anterior horn degeneration; infants are floppy with tongue fasciculations and absent reflexes.
notes.why: Descending upper motor neuron pathways normally inhibit spinal stretch reflex circuits, so losing them releases the reflex arc and produces spasticity, hyperreflexia, and an extensor plantar response. A lower motor neuron lesion cuts the efferent limb of the reflex itself, so tone and reflexes fall. Denervated muscle fibers lose trophic support and atrophy markedly, and irritable, dying motor neurons fire spontaneously as fasciculations. ALS mixes both pictures because it destroys neurons on both sides of the anterior horn synapse while sparing sensory neurons.

points: Somatic motor is one neuron from the CNS to skeletal muscle; ACh acts on nicotinic (NM) receptors and is always excitatory.
Visceral motor is a two-neuron chain: a myelinated preganglionic neuron in the CNS synapses in an autonomic ganglion on an unmyelinated postganglionic neuron.
Visceral targets are smooth muscle, cardiac muscle, and glands, and the effect can excite or inhibit.
The adrenal medulla is the exception: preganglionic sympathetic fibers end directly on chromaffin cells, which act as modified postganglionic neurons.
notes.why: Skeletal muscle has no intrinsic activity, so the somatic motor neuron's ACh opens nicotinic ligand-gated cation channels, depolarizes the end plate, and always excites. Visceral targets already have their own tone or rhythm, so autonomic input modulates them, and the postganglionic transmitter and the receptor subtype on the target decide whether the effect is excitation or inhibition. Chromaffin cells arise from neural crest like postganglionic neurons, which is why preganglionic fibers reach them directly and they release catecholamines into the blood as hormones.

points: Subacute combined degeneration (vitamin B12 deficiency): dorsal columns plus lateral corticospinal tracts, with spinocerebellar tracts often involved.
Tabes dorsalis (tertiary syphilis): dorsal columns and dorsal roots, so sensory ataxia, positive Romberg sign, lightning pains, and lost reflexes.
Anterior spinal artery infarct: anterior two thirds of the cord; bilateral spastic weakness and pain and temperature loss below the level, with vibration and position sense spared.
Complete transection: loss of all motor and sensory function below the level, with spinal shock (flaccid, areflexic) first and UMN signs below the level later.
At the level of any cord lesion, damage to anterior horn cells adds LMN signs in that segment.
notes.why: Each named syndrome reflects the blood supply or the vulnerability of specific columns. B12 deficiency disrupts myelin maintenance, so the long, heavily myelinated dorsal column and corticospinal axons fail first, while Treponema pallidum damages the dorsal roots and cuts the afferent limb of the stretch reflex, so tabes loses reflexes. The anterior spinal artery supplies the anterior two thirds of the cord while paired posterior spinal arteries supply the dorsal columns, so an anterior infarct spares vibration and position sense. After acute transection, sudden loss of descending facilitation silences spinal reflex circuits (spinal shock) until they reorganize and spasticity appears.

points: Visceral pain fibers travel back with sympathetic nerves to the T1 to L2 dorsal root ganglia, which is why organ pain is referred to the matching dermatomes.
Examples: heart pain to T1 to T4 (chest and medial left arm); early appendicitis to T10 (periumbilical).
Pain from pelvic organs below the pelvic pain line travels with the pelvic splanchnic (parasympathetic) nerves to S2 to S4.
Reflex afferents travel with parasympathetic nerves: carotid sinus baroreceptors by CN IX and aortic arch baroreceptors by CN X.
Both end in the nucleus solitarius (nucleus tractus solitarius) in the medulla, which adjusts vagal and sympathetic output.
notes.why: Visceral afferents are sparse and converge on the same dorsal horn neurons that receive somatic input from particular dermatomes, so the brain attributes the pain to that skin area (referred pain). Because visceral pain fibers follow sympathetic routes, the referral level tracks the organ's sympathetic segment, such as T10 for the appendix. Reflex afferents instead run with CN IX and CN X to the nucleus tractus solitarius, which compares the incoming pressure signal with a set point and adjusts vagal and sympathetic output beat by beat.

tricks.label: Cross point decides the side
tricks.text: Find where the lesion sits relative to the pyramidal decussation. Above it (cortex, capsule, brainstem), the weakness is on the opposite side. Below it (spinal cord), the weakness is on the same side.

tricks.label: Back of the cord is the B12 and syphilis zone
tricks.text: Both B12 deficiency and syphilis hit the dorsal columns. Add spastic signs (corticospinal) and you have B12. Add lost reflexes and lightning pains (dorsal roots) and you have tabes.

tricks.label: Pain goes with sympathetics, reflexes go with parasympathetics
tricks.text: Visceral pain fibers ride sympathetic nerves to T1 to L2 and refer to those dermatomes. Baroreceptor and chemoreceptor fibers ride CN IX and CN X to the nucleus solitarius.

highYield: The lateral corticospinal tract runs in the posterior limb of the internal capsule and crosses at the caudal medulla.
ALS is the classic disease with UMN and LMN signs in the same patient and no sensory loss.
Polio and spinal muscular atrophy give pure LMN signs from anterior horn cell loss.
Anterior spinal artery infarct spares vibration and position sense because the posterior spinal arteries supply the dorsal columns.
Vitamin B12 deficiency damages dorsal columns and lateral corticospinal tracts (subacute combined degeneration).
Carotid sinus afferents travel in CN IX and aortic arch afferents in CN X; both reach the nucleus solitarius.
Somatic motor uses one neuron and nicotinic receptors; visceral motor uses two neurons and a ganglion.
pitfalls: Babinski sign and brisk reflexes point to UMN damage; fasciculations and atrophy point to LMN damage. ALS has both, so mixed signs are the clue.
Right after a cord injury, spinal shock looks like an LMN lesion (flaccid, areflexic). UMN signs appear below the level over days to weeks.
Tabes dorsalis gives lost reflexes because the dorsal roots are damaged; subacute combined degeneration usually gives Babinski signs because the corticospinal tracts are damaged.
Visceral pain from most organs uses sympathetic pathways, but pain from pelvic organs below the pelvic pain line uses the pelvic splanchnic nerves.

summary: The twelve cranial nerves, the brachial plexus, the major limb nerves, and the dermatomes. Exam questions give a deficit, such as a down-and-out eye, a wrist drop, or a numb lateral foot, and ask which nerve, root, or site is injured.

points: CN III palsy: eye down and out, ptosis, and a dilated pupil; a compressing posterior communicating artery aneurysm affects the pupil early.
CN IV palsy: vertical diplopia worse looking down and in (stairs, reading); the patient tilts the head away from the lesion.
CN VI palsy: the eye cannot abduct and drifts medially, giving horizontal diplopia.
CN V3 lesion: jaw deviates toward the weak side; CN X lesion: uvula deviates away from the lesion.
CN XII lesion: tongue deviates toward the lesion because the intact genioglossus pushes it over.
CN XI lesion: weak shoulder shrug on the same side and weak head turn to the opposite side.
notes.why: Each sign follows from which muscle is lost and which is left unopposed. With CN III out, the intact lateral rectus and superior oblique pull the eye down and out, and loss of the levator palpebrae and parasympathetic pupillary fibers gives ptosis and mydriasis. The pupillary fibers run on the outside of the nerve, so aneurysm compression dilates the pupil early, while ischemic (diabetic) palsy damages the core and usually spares it. A weak genioglossus lets the tongue drift toward the lesion, while intact palatal muscles pull the uvula away from a CN X lesion.

points: Motor neurons for the upper face get input from both hemispheres; neurons for the lower face get input mainly from the opposite hemisphere.
UMN lesion (stroke in cortex or internal capsule): weakness of the contralateral lower face only, forehead spared.
CN VII lesion (Bell palsy): weakness of the whole ipsilateral face, including the forehead and eye closure.
Depending on the site, a CN VII lesion can also cause hyperacusis (stapedius), lost taste on the anterior two thirds of the tongue, and less tearing.
notes.why: The facial motor nucleus has an upper-face part that receives corticobulbar input from both hemispheres and a lower-face part that receives input mainly from the opposite hemisphere. A cortical or capsular lesion removes only one source of input, so the bilaterally supplied forehead keeps working while the contralateral lower face droops. A lesion of the nucleus or nerve removes the final common pathway for the whole half of the face. The extra findings localize along the nerve's course, because the greater petrosal nerve (tearing), the nerve to stapedius, and the chorda tympani (taste) branch at different points in the temporal bone.

points: Roots C5 to T1, three trunks (upper C5 to C6, middle C7, lower C8 to T1), anterior and posterior divisions, three cords, five terminal branches.
Cords are named by their relation to the axillary artery: lateral, posterior, medial.
Erb palsy (upper trunk, C5 to C6): arm adducted, internally rotated, elbow extended, forearm pronated (waiter's tip).
Klumpke palsy (lower trunk, C8 to T1): claw hand from loss of intrinsic hand muscles, sometimes with Horner syndrome from T1 damage.
Axillary nerve (surgical neck fracture, anterior shoulder dislocation): weak deltoid abduction and numb lateral shoulder.
Radial nerve (midshaft humerus fracture): wrist drop and numb dorsum of the hand near the thumb.
Median nerve (carpal tunnel or supracondylar fracture): thenar weakness and numb lateral three and a half fingers on the palm.
Ulnar nerve (medial epicondyle fracture, hook of hamate): weak interossei, clawing of fingers 4 and 5, numb medial one and a half fingers.
Long thoracic nerve (C5 to C7, axillary surgery): serratus anterior paralysis with a winged scapula.
notes.why: Plexus injuries follow the mechanics of traction. Forcing the head away from the shoulder stretches the upper trunk (C5 to C6), so the deltoid, rotator cuff external rotators, and biceps fail, and the arm falls into adduction, internal rotation, extension, and pronation. Pulling the arm upward stretches the lower trunk (C8 to T1), which supplies the intrinsic hand muscles, so the lumbricals can no longer flex the MCP joints and extend the IP joints, producing a claw. Distal injuries match the bone each nerve wraps: the axillary nerve at the surgical neck, the radial nerve in the spiral groove, and the ulnar nerve behind the medial epicondyle.

points: Common fibular nerve wraps the fibular neck; injury there gives foot drop, steppage gait, and numb dorsum of foot and lateral leg.
Tibial nerve: loss of plantar flexion and inversion and a numb sole.
Femoral nerve (L2 to L4): weak knee extension, reduced patellar reflex, numb anterior thigh and medial leg.
Obturator nerve (L2 to L4): weak thigh adduction and numb medial thigh, as after pelvic surgery or a difficult vaginal delivery.
Superior gluteal nerve: weak gluteus medius and minimus; standing on the affected leg makes the pelvis drop on the opposite side (Trendelenburg sign).
notes.why: Lower limb deficits follow each nerve's muscle compartment. The common fibular nerve is superficial and tethered where it winds around the fibular neck, so injury there paralyzes the anterior compartment (dorsiflexors) and lateral compartment (evertors), causing foot drop and a high-stepping gait to clear the toes. The tibial nerve supplies the posterior compartment, so its loss removes plantar flexion and inversion. The superior gluteal nerve supplies the hip abductors that hold the pelvis level during single-leg stance, which is why the opposite side of the pelvis sags when the affected leg bears weight.

points: Landmarks: C6 thumb, T4 nipple, T10 umbilicus, L4 knee and medial leg, L5 dorsum of foot, S1 lateral foot.
Matching reflexes: biceps C5 to C6, triceps C7, patellar L4, Achilles S1.
A posterolateral L4 to L5 disc herniation usually compresses the L5 root; L5 to S1 compresses S1.
notes.why: A dermatome is the strip of skin supplied by one dorsal root, and a myotome and a reflex arc share that same root, so a root lesion gives a matched set of sensory loss, weakness, and a reduced reflex. In the lumbar spine each root exits below the pedicle of its own vertebra, and a typical posterolateral herniation misses the root exiting at that level and catches the root descending toward the next foramen. That is why an L4 to L5 herniation affects L5 (weak dorsiflexion and great toe extension) and an L5 to S1 herniation affects S1 (lateral foot, lost Achilles reflex).

points: The MLF links the abducens nucleus on one side to the medial rectus subnucleus of the opposite oculomotor nucleus for conjugate lateral gaze.
MLF lesion: the eye on the lesion side fails to adduct on lateral gaze, and the opposite abducting eye shows nystagmus.
Convergence is preserved because it does not use the MLF.
Bilateral INO in a young adult strongly suggests multiple sclerosis; in an older adult, a brainstem stroke is more likely.
notes.why: The abducens nucleus holds motor neurons to the ipsilateral lateral rectus and interneurons whose axons cross and ascend in the contralateral MLF to the medial rectus subnucleus, which yokes the two eyes in lateral gaze. Cutting the MLF stops the command to the medial rectus, so the eye on the lesion side fails to adduct while the other eye abducts with nystagmus. Convergence uses a separate midbrain pathway that drives the medial rectus directly, so preserved convergence proves CN III and the muscle are intact. MS plaques favor this heavily myelinated tract, which is why bilateral INO in a young adult suggests demyelination.

tricks.text: Peroneal (common fibular) Everts and Dorsiflexes, so injury gives foot dropPED. Tibial Inverts and Plantarflexes, so injury means you cannot stand on your TIPtoes.

tricks.label: Forehead test
tricks.text: Ask the patient to raise the eyebrows. Forehead works: think central lesion (stroke). Forehead weak too: think CN VII itself (Bell palsy).

tricks.label: Lick your wounds
tricks.text: With a CN XII lesion the tongue points toward the bad side, as if licking a wound there. The uvula does the opposite and points away from a CN X lesion.

highYield: A dilated pupil with a down-and-out eye and ptosis means CN III compression, classically by a posterior communicating artery aneurysm.
Forehead sparing means an upper motor neuron facial lesion; forehead involvement means a CN VII lesion.
Erb palsy is upper trunk (C5 to C6) with waiter's tip; Klumpke palsy is lower trunk (C8 to T1) with claw hand.
Midshaft humerus fracture injures the radial nerve and causes wrist drop.
Fibular neck fracture injures the common fibular nerve and causes foot drop.
In a positive Trendelenburg sign, the pelvis drops on the side opposite the injured superior gluteal nerve.
C6 thumb, T4 nipple, T10 umbilicus, L4 knee, L5 dorsum of foot, S1 lateral foot.
INO: the eye on the side of the MLF lesion cannot adduct, convergence is intact, and bilateral INO suggests MS.
pitfalls: Tongue deviates toward a CN XII lesion, but the uvula deviates away from a CN X lesion.
Trendelenburg sign: the dropped hip is on the healthy side, and the weak gluteus medius is on the stance side.
Ptosis in CN III palsy is marked (levator palpebrae); ptosis in Horner syndrome is mild (superior tarsal muscle).
INO is named for the side of the MLF lesion, which is the side of the eye that fails to adduct; the nystagmus appears in the opposite, abducting eye.

summary: The layout of sympathetic and parasympathetic outflow, the transmitters and receptors at each synapse, and two classic clinical pictures: Horner syndrome and autonomic dysreflexia. Exam questions ask you to trace a pathway to find a lesion or to predict a response from a receptor and its G protein.

points: Preganglionic cell bodies sit in the intermediolateral cell column (lateral horn) from T1 to L2, so the system is called thoracolumbar.
Axons leave in the ventral root, enter the white ramus, and synapse in a paravertebral chain ganglion or pass through as splanchnic nerves.
Splanchnic nerves synapse in prevertebral ganglia (celiac, superior mesenteric, inferior mesenteric).
Preganglionic fibers are short and postganglionic fibers are long; gray rami return postganglionic fibers to every spinal nerve.
notes.why: Sympathetic preganglionic neurons exist only in the T1 to L2 lateral horn, so fibers bound for the head, limbs, and pelvis must enter the chain and travel up or down it before synapsing. White rami carry myelinated preganglionic fibers out and exist only at T1 to L2, while gray rami carry unmyelinated postganglionic fibers back to all 31 pairs of spinal nerves for sweat glands, arrector pili, and blood vessels. Ganglia close to the cord let one preganglionic neuron diverge onto many postganglionic neurons, which suits a widespread, coordinated fight-or-flight response.

points: Craniosacral: brainstem nuclei of CN III, VII, IX, and X, plus the S2 to S4 lateral gray matter.
Ganglia lie near or in the target organ, so preganglionic fibers are long and postganglionic fibers are short.
The vagus supplies the thoracic organs and gut up to about the distal transverse colon; pelvic splanchnic nerves (S2 to S4) supply the rest of the colon, bladder, and erectile tissue.
notes.why: Parasympathetic preganglionic fibers travel almost all the way to the target before synapsing, so each response stays local, such as constricting a pupil without changing gut motility. Cranial outflow uses the nerves whose brainstem nuclei hold the preganglionic cells, for example the Edinger-Westphal nucleus for CN III and the dorsal motor nucleus of the vagus for CN X. The vagal territory ends near the junction of the proximal two thirds and distal third of the transverse colon, the midgut to hindgut boundary, and the hindgut and pelvic organs take pelvic splanchnic fibers from S2 to S4. This is why sacral cord injury disrupts bladder emptying and erection.

points: All preganglionic neurons (sympathetic and parasympathetic) release ACh onto nicotinic (NN) receptors in the ganglia.
Parasympathetic postganglionic neurons release ACh onto muscarinic receptors.
Most sympathetic postganglionic neurons release norepinephrine onto adrenergic receptors.
Sweat glands are the exception: sympathetic postganglionic fibers release ACh onto muscarinic receptors.
Adrenal medulla chromaffin cells, driven by preganglionic ACh, release mostly epinephrine into the blood.
G proteins: alpha1 Gq, alpha2 Gi, beta1 and beta2 Gs, M1 Gq, M2 Gi, M3 Gq.
notes.why: Ganglionic nicotinic (NN) receptors are ligand-gated cation channels, so transmission through every ganglion is fast and excitatory. At the target the effect depends on the receptor's G protein: Gq activates phospholipase C to make IP3 and DAG and raises intracellular calcium, Gs activates adenylyl cyclase and raises cAMP, and Gi inhibits adenylyl cyclase. In the SA node, M2 also opens potassium channels through G protein beta-gamma subunits, which slows pacemaker firing. Sweat glands receive cholinergic sympathetic fibers, so anticholinergic drugs cause hot, dry skin.

points: First-order neuron: hypothalamus down the brainstem and cord to the ciliospinal center at C8 to T2.
Second-order (preganglionic) neuron: exits at T1, passes over the lung apex, and ascends the chain to the superior cervical ganglion.
Third-order (postganglionic) neuron: runs on the internal carotid artery (carotid plexus) to the dilator pupillae and superior tarsal muscle.
Loss gives ptosis (mild), miosis, and anhidrosis on the same side.
Pancoast tumor at the lung apex compresses the second-order neuron, often with arm pain and hand weakness from the lower brachial plexus.
Internal carotid dissection injures the third-order neuron, giving painful Horner syndrome; facial sweating is largely spared because those fibers follow the external carotid.
notes.why: The oculosympathetic pathway is a three-neuron chain, and a break at any link removes sympathetic tone on the same side. The superior tarsal muscle normally adds a few millimeters of lid elevation, so its loss gives mild ptosis, and the unopposed pupillary sphincter gives miosis that is most obvious in dim light. Sweat fibers for the face leave with branches of the external carotid artery, so lesions before the carotid bifurcation (first and second order) cause facial anhidrosis, while lesions on the internal carotid largely spare it.

points: Occurs with spinal cord injury at or above T6, above the major splanchnic outflow.
A stimulus below the lesion (full bladder, constipation, pressure sore) triggers a spinal sympathetic reflex.
Descending inhibition cannot cross the lesion, so splanchnic vasoconstriction goes unopposed and blood pressure rises sharply.
Baroreceptors sense the rise and drive vagal reflex bradycardia, which cannot lower the pressure.
Above the lesion: pounding headache, flushing, sweating; below the lesion: pale, cool skin. Removing the trigger (emptying the bladder) ends the episode.
notes.why: Below a high cord lesion, sympathetic preganglionic neurons are cut off from supraspinal control yet still respond to segmental afferent input. A noxious stimulus such as bladder distension triggers a massive spinal sympathetic reflex, and because the large splanchnic vascular bed receives its outflow from segments below T6, widespread vasoconstriction drives blood pressure up. Baroreceptors detect the rise, and the brainstem responds with vagal bradycardia and vasodilation above the lesion, but inhibitory signals cannot descend past the injury, so the pressure stays high until the trigger is removed.

highYield: Sympathetic is thoracolumbar (T1 to L2); parasympathetic is craniosacral (CN III, VII, IX, X and S2 to S4).
Every autonomic ganglion uses ACh on nicotinic receptors.
Sympathetic fibers to sweat glands release ACh onto muscarinic receptors.
Alpha1 and M3 use Gq; alpha2 and M2 use Gi; beta receptors use Gs.
Horner syndrome: ipsilateral ptosis, miosis, and anhidrosis from a break anywhere in the three-neuron oculosympathetic chain.
Pancoast tumor causes Horner syndrome by compressing the preganglionic neuron at the lung apex.
Parotid secretion comes from CN IX through the otic ganglion; tears come from CN VII through the pterygopalatine ganglion.
Autonomic dysreflexia needs a cord lesion at or above T6 and shows severe hypertension with reflex bradycardia.
pitfalls: The parotid is the one major salivary gland driven by CN IX; the submandibular and sublingual glands are driven by CN VII.
Pupil dilation is alpha1 on the dilator muscle; pupil constriction is M3 on the sphincter muscle.
In autonomic dysreflexia the bradycardia is a normal baroreceptor response; the problem is that the brain cannot send inhibition down past the lesion to the blood vessels.
Anhidrosis of the face is prominent with first- and second-order Horner lesions and largely absent with lesions on the internal carotid.

summary: The arteries that feed the brain and spinal cord, the path of cerebrospinal fluid, venous drainage, and how cerebral blood flow is kept steady. Exam questions give a stroke picture and ask for the vessel, show a ventricle pattern and ask where CSF is blocked, or ask what raised intracranial pressure does to perfusion.

points: Anterior supply: each internal carotid artery gives the anterior cerebral artery (ACA) and middle cerebral artery (MCA).
Posterior supply: the two vertebral arteries join to form the basilar artery, which ends by dividing into the posterior cerebral arteries (PCA).
The anterior communicating artery joins the two ACAs; each posterior communicating artery joins an internal carotid to a PCA.
Vertebral branches: PICA and the anterior spinal artery. Basilar branches: AICA, pontine arteries, superior cerebellar artery.
Lenticulostriate arteries come off the proximal MCA and supply the basal ganglia and internal capsule.
notes.why: The circle of Willis joins the carotid and vertebrobasilar systems, so a slowly developing occlusion proximal to the circle can be compensated through the communicating arteries when they are well developed. Penetrating branches distal to the circle are end arteries, and cortical territories overlap only at their borders, so a sudden occlusion beyond the circle causes a predictable territorial infarct. The lenticulostriate arteries are thin perforators that branch sharply from the MCA and receive the full pressure of a large parent artery, which explains why chronic hypertension damages them.

points: ACA: medial frontal and parietal lobes, including the leg and foot area of motor and sensory cortex.
MCA: most of the lateral hemisphere, including face and arm cortex, Broca area, and Wernicke area.
PCA: occipital lobe and inferior temporal lobe; occlusion gives contralateral homonymous hemianopia with macular sparing.
Macular sparing happens because the occipital pole often gets collateral flow from the MCA.
Lenticulostriate occlusion causes a lacunar infarct; in the posterior limb of the internal capsule it gives pure motor hemiparesis.
Lacunar strokes are linked to chronic hypertension and hyaline arteriolosclerosis.
notes.why: The motor and sensory homunculi lie across two arterial territories: the leg and foot area sits on the medial surface fed by the ACA, while the face, arm, and dominant-hemisphere language areas sit on the lateral convexity fed by the MCA. The pattern of weakness (leg more than arm, or face and arm more than leg) therefore names the artery. Chronic hypertension causes hyaline arteriolosclerosis and lipohyalinosis that narrow and occlude small perforators, and a lacune in the internal capsule catches tightly packed corticospinal and corticobulbar fibers without touching cortex, so there is no aphasia, neglect, or field loss.

points: PICA (or vertebral) occlusion: lateral medullary syndrome with dysphagia and hoarseness (nucleus ambiguus), vertigo, ipsilateral Horner syndrome, ipsilateral face and contralateral body pain and temperature loss.
Anterior spinal artery occlusion in the medulla: medial medullary syndrome with contralateral hemiparesis, contralateral loss of vibration and position sense, and ipsilateral tongue deviation.
AICA occlusion: lateral pontine syndrome with ipsilateral facial paralysis and ipsilateral hearing loss on top of the lateral brainstem signs.
Basilar occlusion of the ventral pons: locked-in syndrome with quadriplegia and loss of speech, while consciousness, blinking, and vertical eye movements remain.
notes.why: Brainstem syndromes follow a medial and lateral rule. Medial structures include the corticospinal tract, the medial lemniscus, and the hypoglossal nucleus and nerve, while lateral structures include the spinothalamic tract, the spinal trigeminal nucleus, the vestibular nuclei, the nucleus ambiguus, and the descending sympathetic fibers. Cranial nerve nuclei act on the same side, while the long tracts have already crossed (spinothalamic, medial lemniscus) or have not yet crossed (corticospinal), so a single lesion gives crossed findings. Locked-in syndrome spares consciousness and vertical gaze because the reticular activating system lies dorsally in the tegmentum and the vertical gaze centers sit in the midbrain.

points: Choroid plexus ependymal cells make about 500 mL of CSF a day; about 150 mL is present at any time.
Path: lateral ventricles, interventricular foramina (of Monro), third ventricle, cerebral aqueduct, fourth ventricle.
CSF leaves the fourth ventricle through the median aperture (Magendie) and two lateral apertures (Luschka) into the subarachnoid space.
Arachnoid granulations return CSF to the dural venous sinuses, mainly the superior sagittal sinus.
Ventricles upstream of a block dilate, and ventricles downstream stay normal (noncommunicating hydrocephalus).
Scarred arachnoid granulations (after meningitis or subarachnoid hemorrhage) dilate all four ventricles (communicating hydrocephalus).
notes.why: The choroid plexus epithelium actively secretes CSF by pumping sodium into the ventricle with chloride and water following, so production continues even when outflow is blocked. CSF must pass through narrow channels, and the cerebral aqueduct is the narrowest, which makes it a common site of congenital obstruction (aqueductal stenosis). Absorption at the arachnoid granulations depends on the pressure difference between CSF and venous sinus blood, so scarred granulations or a rise in sinus pressure raises ICP and enlarges all the ventricles.

points: Superficial cerebral veins drain to the superior sagittal sinus through bridging veins that cross the subdural space.
Deep veins join the great cerebral vein, which joins the inferior sagittal sinus to form the straight sinus.
Sinuses meet at the confluence, then flow through the transverse and sigmoid sinuses to the internal jugular vein at the jugular foramen.
Torn bridging veins cause a subdural hematoma: crescent-shaped, crosses suture lines, common in older adults with brain atrophy.
Dural sinus thrombosis blocks venous outflow and CSF absorption, raising ICP; causes include pregnancy, oral contraceptives, dehydration, and thrombophilia.
notes.why: Cerebral veins and dural sinuses have no valves and drain toward the internal jugular veins along pressure gradients. Bridging veins are stretched as the brain shrinks with age or chronic alcohol use, so modest acceleration and deceleration can tear them and bleed slowly into the subdural space, which is not limited by suture lines. Because CSF is absorbed into the superior sagittal sinus, thrombosis there raises both venous pressure and ICP, and the back pressure can cause venous infarcts that often turn hemorrhagic.

points: Autoregulation keeps cerebral blood flow steady over a mean arterial pressure of about 60 to 150 mm Hg.
PaCO2 is the strongest local control: hypercapnia dilates cerebral arterioles and raises flow; hypocapnia from hyperventilation constricts them and lowers flow and ICP.
Low PaO2 dilates cerebral vessels only when it falls below about 50 mm Hg.
Cerebral perfusion pressure equals MAP minus ICP; normal ICP is about 5 to 15 mm Hg.
Cushing reflex: rising ICP lowers perfusion, brainstem ischemia triggers a sympathetic surge that raises MAP, baroreceptors then slow the heart, and brainstem compression makes breathing irregular.
notes.why: Cerebral arterioles constrict when pressure rises and dilate when it falls (myogenic autoregulation), which keeps flow constant within the autoregulatory range. CO2 crosses the blood-brain barrier and lowers perivascular pH, which relaxes arteriolar smooth muscle, and hyperventilation reverses this to lower cerebral blood volume and ICP within minutes. Because the skull is a fixed volume (Monro-Kellie doctrine), any added mass raises ICP, and perfusion pressure falls as ICP approaches MAP. The Cushing triad of hypertension, bradycardia, and irregular respiration signals brainstem ischemia or compression and possible herniation.

pitfalls: Lateral medullary syndrome causes crossed findings: pain and temperature loss on the same side of the face and the opposite side of the body.

summary: The association cortex is the part of the cortex that plans behavior, directs attention, handles language, and recognizes what we see. Exam questions describe a behavior or speech pattern after a stroke or degeneration and ask you to name the damaged area, or match an EEG pattern to a sleep stage.

points: Handles executive function: planning, working memory, judgment, impulse control, and personality.
Dorsolateral damage causes poor planning, apathy, and perseveration.
Orbitofrontal damage causes disinhibition, impulsive and socially inappropriate behavior.
Frontotemporal dementia begins with personality change, disinhibition, apathy, or language decline while memory is relatively spared early.
FTD shows frontal and temporal atrophy; some cases have tau inclusions called Pick bodies.
notes.why: The prefrontal cortex holds goals in working memory and, through loops with the basal ganglia, thalamus, and limbic system, selects appropriate actions and suppresses inappropriate ones. Dorsolateral circuits support planning and shifting between strategies, so damage causes apathy, poor organization, and perseveration on an old response. Orbitofrontal circuits link behavior to reward and social context, so damage releases impulsive, disinhibited behavior. In frontotemporal dementia, neurodegeneration with tau or TDP-43 inclusions targets these frontal and anterior temporal networks first, so behavior changes before memory fails.

points: Posterior parietal cortex builds a map of space and directs attention within it.
The right parietal lobe attends to both sides of space, while the left attends mostly to the right side.
A right (nondominant) parietal lesion therefore causes left hemispatial neglect: the patient ignores the left side of the body and the world.
A dominant (usually left) angular gyrus lesion causes Gerstmann syndrome: agraphia, acalculia, finger agnosia, and left-right confusion.
notes.why: The posterior parietal cortex combines visual, somatosensory, and vestibular input into a body-centered map of space and directs attention within it. Because the right hemisphere attends to both halves of space and the left attends mainly to the right half, a left lesion is compensated by the intact right side, while a right lesion leaves the left half of space with little attention. The dominant angular gyrus integrates written symbols, numbers, and the body schema with language, which is why its damage produces the four linked deficits of Gerstmann syndrome.

points: Broca area (dominant inferior frontal gyrus) plans speech output.
Wernicke area (dominant posterior superior temporal gyrus) handles comprehension.
The arcuate fasciculus connects Wernicke area to Broca area and is needed for repetition.
Broca aphasia: nonfluent, effortful speech with intact comprehension; patients know their errors.
Wernicke aphasia: fluent but meaningless speech with poor comprehension; patients are often unaware.
Conduction aphasia: fluent speech and good comprehension but poor repetition.
Global aphasia: large dominant MCA stroke damaging all three, so speech, comprehension, and repetition all fail.
notes.why: Language runs as a network in the dominant hemisphere: Wernicke area decodes heard words into meaning, the arcuate fasciculus carries the word pattern forward, and Broca area turns it into a motor plan for the adjacent face and larynx motor cortex. Broca lesions break output, so speech is slow and effortful, and contralateral face and arm weakness often occurs because the motor strip is nearby. Wernicke lesions break comprehension, including the ability to monitor one's own speech, so output stays fluent but meaningless. Repetition fails whenever the loop between the two areas is cut, which is why it is the key test for conduction aphasia.

points: Dorsal stream (occipitoparietal) answers where: spatial location, motion, and visually guided reaching.
Ventral stream (occipitotemporal) answers what: object, color, and face recognition.
Fusiform gyrus damage on the ventral surface causes prosopagnosia, the inability to recognize familiar faces.
Dorsal stream damage impairs motion perception and accurate reaching toward seen objects.
notes.why: Both streams start in primary visual cortex and divide the work of vision. The dorsal stream projects to posterior parietal cortex and includes the motion area MT (V5), so it computes where an object is, how it moves, and how to reach for it. The ventral stream runs through the inferior temporal lobe, where the fusiform face area matches the shape of a face to a stored identity. Because these areas are anatomically separate, a lesion can abolish one function, such as face recognition, while the other, such as accurate reaching, remains intact.

points: Awake and alert: beta waves (fast, low voltage). Awake, relaxed, eyes closed: alpha waves.
N1: theta waves, light sleep. N2: sleep spindles and K complexes; the largest share of the night.
N3: delta waves (slow, high voltage), deep slow-wave sleep, most common in the first third of the night.
REM: low-voltage mixed activity that looks like the awake EEG, with rapid eye movements, muscle atonia, and dreaming.
REM periods lengthen toward morning.
notes.why: The scalp EEG records the summed postsynaptic potentials of cortical pyramidal neurons, so its pattern reflects how synchronized those neurons are. Alert attention desynchronizes the cortex into fast, low-voltage beta activity, while deepening non-REM sleep lets thalamocortical circuits oscillate together, producing spindles and K complexes in N2 and slow, high-voltage delta waves in N3. REM is generated by pontine cholinergic activity that desynchronizes the cortex much like waking, while descending brainstem inhibition of spinal motor neurons produces atonia.

summary: The hypothalamus controls temperature, appetite, water balance, and daily rhythms, and the limbic system handles memory and emotion. Exam questions link a lesion to a change in eating, temperature, memory, or behavior, and test the mechanism of fever and the common sleep disorders.

points: Supraoptic and paraventricular nuclei make ADH and oxytocin, which travel down axons to the posterior pituitary.
Arcuate nucleus releases dopamine (inhibits prolactin) and GHRH into the portal system.
Lateral nucleus drives hunger; lesions cause anorexia and weight loss.
Ventromedial nucleus signals satiety; lesions cause hyperphagia and obesity, as with a craniopharyngioma.
Leptin from fat cells stimulates satiety pathways and inhibits hunger pathways.
Anterior hypothalamus drives heat loss (sweating, vasodilation); lesions cause hyperthermia.
Posterior hypothalamus drives heat conservation (shivering, vasoconstriction); lesions cause hypothermia.
notes.why: Each hypothalamic region compares a sensed variable with a set point and corrects it through hormones, autonomic output, and behavior. Supraoptic and paraventricular neurons release ADH and oxytocin from their own axon terminals in the posterior pituitary, while arcuate neurons release dopamine and GHRH into the portal veins of the anterior pituitary. Paired centers explain the lesion signs: destroying the ventromedial satiety center unmasks hunger, destroying the lateral feeding center abolishes it, and the anterior and posterior regions balance heat loss against heat conservation. Leptin reports fat stores to the arcuate nucleus, lowering appetite as fat mass rises.

points: Pyrogens such as bacterial LPS cause macrophages to release IL-1, IL-6, and TNF-alpha.
These cytokines act near the preoptic anterior hypothalamus, where the blood-brain barrier is leaky, and induce COX-2.
COX-2 makes prostaglandin E2, which raises the hypothalamic set point.
Body temperature now sits below the new set point, so the person feels cold, shivers, and vasoconstricts until temperature rises, for example from 37 °C (98.6 °F) to 39 °C (102.2 °F).
When the set point falls back, the person sweats and vasodilates.
Hyperthermia (heat stroke) differs: the set point is normal and heat gain exceeds heat loss.
notes.why: Fever is a regulated rise in the set point, which separates it from hyperthermia. Circulating IL-1, IL-6, and TNF-alpha act at the organum vasculosum of the lamina terminalis (OVLT), a circumventricular area with a leaky blood-brain barrier near the preoptic area, and induce COX-2 and PGE2 synthesis. PGE2 binds EP3 receptors on preoptic neurons and raises the set point, so heat-conserving responses run until core temperature matches it. NSAIDs lower fever by blocking COX but do little in heat stroke, because no set-point change is involved.

points: Parts: hippocampus, amygdala, cingulate gyrus, fornix, mammillary bodies, anterior thalamic nucleus.
Papez circuit: hippocampus, fornix, mammillary bodies, mammillothalamic tract, anterior thalamus, cingulate gyrus, back to the hippocampus.
Bilateral hippocampal damage causes anterograde amnesia: new facts cannot be stored, old memories remain.
Thiamine deficiency (often alcohol use disorder) damages the mammillary bodies and medial thalamus.
Wernicke encephalopathy is confusion, ophthalmoplegia, and ataxia; Korsakoff syndrome adds lasting amnesia with confabulation.
Bilateral amygdala damage (for example HSV-1 encephalitis) causes Kluver-Bucy syndrome: hyperorality, hypersexuality, docility, and visual agnosia.
notes.why: The hippocampus binds new experiences into declarative memory traces that are consolidated into neocortex over time, so bilateral hippocampal damage blocks new memories while older ones survive. The mammillary bodies and medial thalamus are diencephalic relays in the same memory system and depend heavily on thiamine pyrophosphate enzymes (pyruvate dehydrogenase, alpha-ketoglutarate dehydrogenase, transketolase), so thiamine deficiency injures them and produces the amnesia of Korsakoff syndrome. The amygdala assigns emotional value and fear to stimuli, so bilateral loss leaves patients placid and unable to judge what is appropriate to eat, touch, or approach.

points: Light hits melanopsin-containing retinal ganglion cells, which signal the suprachiasmatic nucleus (SCN) through the retinohypothalamic tract.
The SCN signals the pineal gland through a sympathetic relay (superior cervical ganglion); darkness raises melatonin and light suppresses it.
Melatonin is made from serotonin, which is made from tryptophan.
Narcolepsy type 1: loss of orexin (hypocretin) neurons in the lateral hypothalamus, with low CSF hypocretin.
Orexin stabilizes wakefulness and keeps REM features out of waking, so its loss gives daytime sleepiness, sleep-onset REM, cataplexy, sleep paralysis, and hypnagogic hallucinations.
Cataplexy is sudden loss of muscle tone triggered by strong emotion such as laughter, with consciousness preserved.
notes.why: The SCN is an intrinsic clock driven by a feedback loop of clock gene transcription that runs near 24 hours, and light resets it daily through the retinohypothalamic tract. Its output reaches the pineal gland through a long sympathetic route (hypothalamus, intermediolateral column, superior cervical ganglion), and norepinephrine released at night activates the enzyme steps that convert serotonin to melatonin. Orexin neurons in the lateral hypothalamus excite the monoaminergic and cholinergic arousal centers, so their loss makes the switch between waking and REM unstable, and REM features such as atonia and dreaming intrude into wakefulness.

points: REM sleep behavior disorder: normal REM atonia is lost, so patients act out dreams, sometimes violently.
REM sleep behavior disorder often precedes Parkinson disease or dementia with Lewy bodies by years.
Sleepwalking and sleep terrors arise from N3, usually in children, in the first third of the night, with no memory of the event.
Nightmares arise from REM, later in the night, and the child remembers the dream.
Restless legs syndrome: an urge to move the legs at rest, worse in the evening and relieved by movement; linked to iron deficiency (low ferritin), kidney disease, and pregnancy.
notes.why: Sleepwalking and sleep terrors are partial arousals out of N3, so the cortex is not fully awake, no memory is recorded, and they cluster early in the night when N3 dominates, while nightmares arise in REM later in the night and are recalled. In REM sleep behavior disorder, alpha-synuclein pathology damages the brainstem nuclei that produce REM atonia, which is why it often heralds a synucleinopathy. Restless legs syndrome is thought to reflect low brain iron, which impairs dopamine synthesis because tyrosine hydroxylase needs iron.

tricks.label: A/C and posterior heater
tricks.text: Anterior hypothalamus is the A/C (cools); posterior hypothalamus is the heater (warms).

tricks.label: Zap the lateral, shrink laterally; zap the ventromedial, grow ventrally and medially
tricks.text: Lateral nucleus lesion causes weight loss (anorexia). Ventromedial nucleus lesion causes overeating and weight gain.

tricks.label: Fever is a thermostat change
tricks.text: In fever, PGE2 turns the thermostat up and the body works to reach it (chills). In heat stroke the thermostat is normal and the body simply cannot shed heat.

highYield: Supraoptic nucleus makes mostly ADH; paraventricular nucleus makes mostly oxytocin.
Ventromedial lesion causes hyperphagia; lateral lesion causes anorexia.
IL-1, IL-6, and TNF-alpha raise the set point through COX-2 and prostaglandin E2.
Bilateral hippocampal damage causes anterograde amnesia.
Thiamine deficiency damages the mammillary bodies and causes Wernicke-Korsakoff syndrome.
Bilateral amygdala damage causes Kluver-Bucy syndrome.
Narcolepsy with cataplexy comes from loss of lateral hypothalamic orexin (hypocretin) neurons.
REM sleep behavior disorder often predicts a later synucleinopathy such as Parkinson disease.
pitfalls: Anterior hypothalamic lesions cause hyperthermia (heat loss center lost); posterior lesions cause hypothermia (heat conservation center lost).
Chills at fever onset mean the set point has risen above body temperature; the hypothalamus is working normally.
Sleep terrors arise from N3 and are not remembered; nightmares arise from REM and are remembered.
Cataplexy keeps consciousness intact, which separates it from a seizure or syncope.

dumps.p: Draw a sagittal view of the hypothalamus and pituitary. Label the supraoptic, paraventricular, arcuate, lateral, ventromedial, anterior, posterior, and suprachiasmatic nuclei and write what each does and what a lesion causes.
l: Supraoptic and paraventricular make ADH and oxytocin for the posterior pituitary
Arcuate releases dopamine and GHRH
Lateral nucleus: hunger; lesion gives anorexia
Ventromedial nucleus: satiety; lesion gives hyperphagia and obesity
Anterior: heat loss; lesion gives hyperthermia
Posterior: heat conservation; lesion gives hypothermia
Suprachiasmatic: circadian rhythm, driven by retinal light input
Lateral hypothalamic orexin neurons lost in narcolepsy

dumps.p: Trace how a bacterial infection raises body temperature. Start with the pathogen and end with shivering, and then show what happens when the fever breaks.
l: Pyrogen such as LPS stimulates macrophages
Macrophages release IL-1, IL-6, and TNF-alpha
Cytokines induce COX-2 near the preoptic anterior hypothalamus
COX-2 makes prostaglandin E2
PGE2 raises the hypothalamic set point
Body is below the new set point, so shivering and vasoconstriction raise temperature
When the set point falls, sweating and vasodilation bring temperature down
Heat stroke differs because the set point stays normal

flows.title: Fever
steps: Pathogen products such as LPS activate macrophages
Macrophages release IL-1, IL-6, and TNF-alpha
Cytokines act at the OVLT near the preoptic hypothalamus
COX-2 induction raises PGE2 synthesis
PGE2 raises the hypothalamic temperature set point
Shivering and vasoconstriction raise core temperature to the new set point

flows.title: Papez circuit
steps: Hippocampus sends output through the fornix
Fornix ends in the mammillary bodies
Mammillothalamic tract carries signals to the anterior thalamic nucleus
Anterior thalamus projects to the cingulate gyrus
Cingulum returns signals through entorhinal cortex to the hippocampus

flows.title: Wernicke-Korsakoff syndrome
steps: Chronic alcohol use reduces thiamine intake and absorption
Thiamine pyrophosphate-dependent enzymes fail (PDH, alpha-ketoglutarate dehydrogenase, transketolase)
Energy failure injures the mammillary bodies and medial thalamus
Acute Wernicke encephalopathy: confusion, ophthalmoplegia, ataxia
Untreated injury leaves Korsakoff syndrome: lasting amnesia with confabulation
